rationale: The button's only content is the Private Use Area codepoint U+E001 rendered as a trash icon; it conveys the 'delete' action but has no aria-label, no visually-hidden text, and no adjacent real label, so it has no accessible name.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...'

rationale: The link's sole content is the PUA codepoint U+F019 (FontAwesome 'download' range) rendered as a download icon; the link has no text alternative, so screen-reader users get no name for the control.
citation: Failure F65: 'Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 due to omitting the alt attribute or text alternative on img elements, area elements, and input elements of type image.' (analogue: a meaningful glyph with no text alternative)

rationale: Every formatting button in the toolbar contains only a bare Private Use Area glyph (U+E100-U+E103) and no aria-label or text, so each control conveys meaning visually but exposes no accessible name to assistive technology.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 condition for 1.1.1: meaningful images/icons require an equivalent text alternative; icon fonts and CSS-generated content that convey meaning need accessible names.

rationale: The PUA codepoint U+F071 rendered as a warning triangle is the only indication that the node is in a degraded state; there is no text alternative, so the status is unavailable to non-visual users.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...'

rationale: The button visibly reads 'Submit' but is built from Cyrillic and superscript homoglyph codepoints (U+0405, U+1D58, U+043C, U+0456) instead of Latin letters, so the computed accessible name is a meaningless lookalike string rather than the real word.
citation: Failure F30: 'Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 and 1.2.1 due to using text alternatives that are not alternatives (e.g., filenames or placeholder text).' (a glyph string that is not the real text)

rationale: The navigation link appears to read 'SHOP' but the H, O, and P are Greek lookalikes (U+0397, U+039F, U+03A1); no accessible name override is supplied, so assistive technology announces a non-word and the link's purpose is lost.
citation: Technique G94: provide a text alternative that presents the same information as the non-text content / equivalent purpose (here the real word 'SHOP' is never exposed as real text).

rationale: The promotional word 'SALE' is spelled with Cyrillic homoglyphs (U+0405, U+0410, U+0415) plus one Latin L; the conveyed information exists only as lookalike glyphs, so a screen reader cannot announce the real word.
citation: Failure F30: 'Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 and 1.2.1 due to using text alternatives that are not alternatives.' (lookalike glyphs are not the real text alternative)

rationale: The anchor has no DOM text; its entire label is delivered by a CSS ::before content:'\f0e0' mail glyph (a PUA codepoint). CSS-generated content conveying meaning with no accessible name leaves the link unnamed for assistive technology.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 condition for 1.1.1: CSS-generated content that conveys meaning needs an accessible name; here the meaning lives only in pseudo-element content.

rationale: The rating element is empty in the DOM; the '4 of 5 stars' value is carried entirely by ::before generated star glyphs (U+2605/U+2606) with no text alternative, so the rating is inaccessible to non-visual users.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...'

rationale: The only indication that the password field is required is a CSS ::after content:' (required)' string; this meaning lives solely in generated content and is not exposed in the DOM or field semantics, so assistive technology never receives the 'required' information.
citation: Technique G95 / G94: text alternatives must present the equivalent information; required-state meaning placed only in CSS content is not a real text alternative.

rationale: The comparison cell is empty in the DOM; a ::before checkmark glyph (U+2714) is the only signal that the feature is included for the Pro plan, with no text alternative, so the included/excluded distinction is invisible to assistive technology.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...'

rationale: The navigation toggle button's only content is the PUA codepoint U+F0C9 rendered as a hamburger menu icon; with no aria-label or text, the control that opens the menu has no accessible name.
citation: Failure F65: 'Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 due to omitting the alt attribute or text alternative...' (analogue: a meaningful icon-font glyph with no text alternative)

rationale: The button still uses the PUA trash glyph U+E001, but aria-label='Delete Quarterly report.pdf' supplies an equivalent text alternative, so the control has an accessible name and the non-text content is named.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...' (satisfied here via aria-label)

rationale: The PUA download glyph is marked aria-hidden='true' so it is ignored by assistive technology, while the adjacent real visible text 'Download' supplies the button's accessible name; the meaning is conveyed by real text.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): non-text content used for pure decoration may be implemented so that it can be ignored by assistive technology (aria-hidden) when adjacent real text carries the meaning.

rationale: The PUA magnifier glyph is aria-hidden and a visually-hidden .sr-only span provides the real text 'Search', giving the button an accessible name while keeping the icon visual-only; the non-text content has an equivalent text alternative.
citation: Technique G94: provide a text alternative that presents the same information; the visually-hidden 'Search' text serves the equivalent purpose of the icon.

rationale: The button label 'Submit' is composed entirely of real Latin letters with no PUA characters, homoglyphs, or CSS-generated content, so there is no glyph substitution and the accessible name equals the visible text.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): the criterion governs non-text content; ordinary real text with an accurate accessible name is not a glyph-substitution failure.

rationale: The ::before bullet glyph (U+2022) is purely decorative; the meaning of every list item is fully carried by the adjacent real text, so the generated glyph conveys no information that lacks a text alternative.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): non-text content that is decoration may be implemented so it can be ignored by assistive technology; a decorative bullet beside real text conveys no unlabeled meaning.

rationale: The ::before content is an empty string used only as a CSS hook for a decorative accent bar; it carries no character glyph and conveys no information, so there is nothing requiring a text alternative.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): non-text content used for decoration may be implemented so that it can be ignored by assistive technology; empty generated content conveys no meaning.

rationale: The decorative star glyphs are wrapped in an aria-hidden span, and the real text '4 out of 5 stars' carries the rating value, so the meaning is available as genuine text and the glyphs are correctly ignored by assistive technology.
citation: Technique G94: provide a text alternative that presents the same information as the non-text content; the '4 out of 5 stars' text serves the equivalent purpose.

rationale: The paragraph uses real Latin words plus genuine typographic punctuation (em-dash U+2014 and curly apostrophe U+2019); these are legitimate text characters, not cross-script lookalikes, so there is no glyph substitution.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): the criterion targets non-text content; ordinary prose with real punctuation is text, not a glyph substituting for a different character.

rationale: The gear glyph is generated via ::before on an <i aria-hidden='true'>, so it is ignored by assistive technology, while the adjacent real text 'Settings' provides the link's accessible name; the meaning is carried by real text.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): decorative non-text content may be implemented so it can be ignored by assistive technology when adjacent real text conveys the meaning.

rationale: The PUA question-circle glyph U+F059 is wrapped in an aria-hidden span while the adjacent real text 'Get help' supplies the link's accessible name, so the icon is decorative-only and the link is properly named.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): non-text content used for decoration may be implemented so it can be ignored by assistive technology; the real 'Get help' text serves the equivalent purpose.

rationale: The name 'Renée Müller' uses legitimate accented Latin letters (U+00E9, U+00FC) that are the correct spelling of the name, not cross-script lookalikes substituting for ASCII; the visible text equals the intended text. A homoglyph detector might flag non-ASCII characters, so abstaining is defensible.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): the criterion concerns non-text content; correctly spelled accented real text is not a glyph substituted for a different character, so no failure applies.

rationale: The link has real text 'Documentation', but a ::after arrow glyph (U+2197) may either be a purely decorative chevron or the only signal that the link opens an external site. Because whether the glyph carries unlabeled meaning is genuinely uncertain, a runner may defensibly abstain rather than decide.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative...'; if the generated arrow conveys an external-link meaning it would need a text alternative, but its informativeness here is ambiguous.

rationale: The weather status icon is delivered as a real element with alt='Rain showers', providing an equivalent text alternative; it is not a PUA character, homoglyph, or CSS-generated glyph, so there is no glyph substitution and the non-text content is named.
citation: Failure F65 (inverse): the alt attribute IS present and meaningful here, so the image's non-text content has the required text alternative and 1.1.1 is satisfied.

rationale: The ::before large quotation-mark glyph (U+201C) is decorative styling on a blockquote whose full meaning is in the real text; the generated glyph adds no information that would require a separate text alternative.
citation: SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): non-text content used purely for decoration may be implemented so it can be ignored by assistive technology; a decorative quote mark over real prose conveys no unlabeled meaning.
